pos: n. (the capital of Bohemia, where Jan Hus preached and where the Bohemian Reformation was both begun and broken)
etymology: Czech Praha, from práh, a threshold or ford-sill, for the rocky shelf in the Vltava at the crossing; Latin Praga, German Prag.
biblical_def: Prague is the city in which the Reformation began a hundred years before Luther and was then extinguished by arms. Charles IV founded its university in 1348, the first north of the Alps, and it was from the university that the Czech reform party drew its learning and from Wyclif's books, carried there by students, that it drew much of its doctrine. Jan Hus preached at the Bethlehem Chapel in the Czech tongue from 1402 until his silencing, and the city stood behind him when Constance burned him in 1415. Prague then produced the Four Articles of 1420, which asked for free preaching, the cup for the laity, the stripping of clerical wealth and the punishment of public sin, and for two centuries the Utraquist consistory in Prague administered a communion in both kinds that Rome tolerated and never approved. The Bohemian Confession of 1575 was drawn up there; the Letter of Majesty of 1609 granted the city's Protestants their liberties; the defenestration of 1618 began the war that ended them. On 21 June 1621 twenty-seven of the kingdom's leading men were executed on the Old Town Square, and the recatholicising of the city followed. The dictionary enters Prague because it shows that a reform can hold a capital, a university and a crown and still be lost when it rests on a nobility's charter rather than on the word preached.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chapel as a house for public worship; a university as an assemblage of colleges; a council as an assembly convened for consultation; and a defenestration as the act of throwing out of a window.
webster_full: CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; a building subordinate to a church, or a private oratory.
UNIVERSITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
DEFENESTRATION, n. The act of throwing out of a window.
CUP, n. A small vessel used to drink out of; the sacramental cup, and by metonymy that which it contains.

Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Mat 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
corruption_summary: Capital of Bohemia, seat of the Bethlehem Chapel and of the Utraquist consistory, where the Czech reform rose in 1402 and was broken on the Old Town Square in 1621.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the settlement by charter, and Prague is the warning. The Letter of Majesty of 1609 gave the Protestant estates their churches, their schools and their consistory under the emperor's own seal, and within eleven years the seal was cut off the parchment and the churches were gone. A reform that locks its gains into a privilege granted by a hostile prince has secured a document, not a church; what secures a church is that ministers preach and congregations are taught, so that when the charter is torn the people still know the doctrine. Prague had the charter and, outside the Unity of Brethren, too little of the teaching.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of the preached word as the church's foundation, tested against Scripture and not against a privilege. The rule by which Hus judged the indulgence-preachers, and by which the Four Articles asked to be judged, is “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20). Prague also shows the other side of the promise: when its ministers were driven out in 1621 they carried the doctrine with them, and “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) describes the Bohemian exile exactly.

pos: n. (the kingdom of the Czechs, the first land in Europe to carry through a reformation, and the first to have one taken away by force)
etymology: Latin Boiohaemum, the home of the Boii, a Celtic people; Czech Čechy; German Böhmen.
biblical_def: Bohemia is the kingdom in which a national reformation was carried, held for two hundred years, and then undone. The burning of Hus in 1415 turned a preaching movement into a nation's cause; the Hussite wars that followed broke five crusades, and the Compacts agreed at Basel and proclaimed in 1436 conceded communion in both kinds to the kingdom, the one formal concession Rome ever made to a reforming body before Trent. Out of the wars came two bodies: the Utraquists, who kept the cup and little else, and the Unity of Brethren, gathered from 1457, who kept a disciplined church with its own ministry, its own hymnody and its own press, and who gave the land the Kralice Bible. The Bohemian Confession of 1575 and the Letter of Majesty of 1609 brought the Lutheran, Utraquist and Brethren parties into one legal settlement. It ended in a single afternoon at White Mountain in November 1620. Thirty thousand families went into exile, the Brethren's press and schools were destroyed, and the land was recatholicised so thoroughly that the Czechs call the age that followed the darkness. The dictionary enters Bohemia because it is the proof that a reformation can be genuinely national, genuinely confessed, and still fail to be rooted, and because the Brethren who survived it became the seed of the modern missionary movement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a kingdom as the territory subject to a king; a compact as an agreement or contract between parties; a remnant as that which is left after a part is taken away; and exile as banishment from one's country.
webster_full: KINGDOM, n. The territory or country subject to a king; an undivided territory under the dominion of a monarch.
COMPACT, n. An agreement; a contract between parties; a word that signifies an agreement for the performance of some act.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country by authority.
UTRAQUIST, n. One who holds that the laity ought to receive the sacrament in both kinds, in bread and in wine.
scriptures: Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations.
corruption_summary: The Czech kingdom, reformed from 1415, settled by the Compacts of 1436 and the Letter of Majesty of 1609, and broken at White Mountain in 1620.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the mistaking of a political victory for a reformation. Bohemia won its wars and got its Compacts, and the Compacts gave the kingdom the cup while leaving the mass, the priesthood, the invocation of saints and purgatory untouched. The Utraquist church that resulted was a church defined by one ceremony and emptied of doctrine, and when the Habsburg pressure came it had almost nothing to resist with. The Unity of Brethren, which had no political settlement at all and was persecuted by Utraquist and Catholic alike, is the body that survived; “there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) is the right description of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the measure of a reformation is doctrine taught and discipline kept, not concessions won. Bohemia's exiles are among those of whom it is written that “they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins” (Heb 11:37), and their land's history is the plainest commentary on the warning that “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12). The kingdom was lost and the church was not, because the church was in the taught people and not in the charter.

pos: n. (the margraviate east of Bohemia, the refuge of the Unity of Brethren and of the Anabaptists, and the cradle of the Moravian missions)
etymology: Latin Moravia, from the river Morava; Czech Morava; German Mähren.
biblical_def: Moravia was a margraviate of the Bohemian crown whose nobility tolerated what Prague would not, and its toleration made it the most crowded refuge in Reformation Europe. The Unity of Brethren had its strongest congregations there, its best schools, and at Kralice the press on which the six-volume Czech Bible was printed between 1579 and 1593, a translation from the Hebrew and Greek that remained the Czech Protestant Bible for three centuries. The Anabaptists expelled from Switzerland, Tyrol and Bavaria settled at Nikolsburg and Austerlitz from 1526, and the communal Hutterite farms in Moravia grew to tens of thousands before the Thirty Years War destroyed them. Moravian lords such as Karel of Zerotin protected ministers whom the emperor had outlawed. The Habsburg victory of 1620 ended it: the Brethren were expelled in 1622, their press broken, Comenius driven abroad, and the land put under a Catholic settlement enforced by its new landlords. What remained was the hidden seed, families who kept the Brethren's books and discipline in secret for a century, until in 1722 a company of them crossed into Upper Lusatia and settled at Herrnhut. The dictionary enters Moravia because that hidden century, and not the toleration before it, is what produced the renewed Brethren and the first sustained Protestant missions.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a margraviate as the territory of a margrave; a refuge as shelter or protection from danger; a seed as that from which a plant grows; and toleration as the allowance of what is not wholly approved.
webster_full: MARGRAVIATE, n. The territory or jurisdiction of a margrave, a title of nobility in Germany.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
SEED, n. The substance, animal or vegetable, which nature prepares for the reproduction and conservation of the species.
TOLERATION, n. The act of tolerating; allowance of that which is not wholly approved; the allowance of religious opinions by law.
DEW, n. The water or moisture collected or deposited on the surface of bodies in the night.
scriptures: Mic 5:7
And the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many people as a dew from the LORD, as the showers upon the grass, that tarrieth not for man, nor waiteth for the sons of men.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
corruption_summary: Margraviate east of Bohemia, refuge of the Brethren and the Hutterites, home of the Kralice press, and the land of the hidden seed that became Herrnhut.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the assumption that a church needs liberty in order to live. Moravia had as much liberty as any land in Europe before 1620 and the Brethren used it well, in schools, a press and a trained ministry; and then it was taken away completely, and the body that the liberty had built went on for a hundred years with no minister, no press and no public meeting. The hidden seed is the answer to the assumption. “the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many people as a dew from the LORD” (Mic 5:7) is dew, not a city wall, and dew falls where nobody has granted it permission.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ordinary means of grace in a family are enough to carry a church across a century when the public means are forbidden. The Moravian families kept the Kralice Bible and the Brethren's catechism and hymns in their houses, taught their children, and produced in 1722 a company that founded Herrnhut and from it the missions to the West Indies, Greenland and the Cape. “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” (Psa 126:6) is the plainest account of what that century was.

pos: n. (the western Bohemian town which held out for Rome through the Hussite wars, and on whose press the first book in Bohemia was printed)
etymology: German Pilsen, Czech Plzeň, probably from a personal name or from plz, a damp place; the royal town was founded about 1295.
biblical_def: Pilsen is the Bohemian town that proves a reformation is not a nation's unanimous act. The second city of the kingdom, it went briefly with the Hussites in 1419 and then turned, and from 1421 it was the Catholic capital of Bohemia and the base from which the crusading armies and the Bohemian Catholic league operated. It was besieged three times and never taken; the last siege, by Prokop the Great in 1433 and 1434, cost the Taborites so much that their field army was fatally weakened before Lipany. Yet the first book printed anywhere in Bohemia came off a Pilsen press about 1476, and the town's printers afterwards worked for both sides, which is the ordinary fact that partisan histories leave out. In 1618 the Protestant estates took the town by storm under Mansfeld, and in 1621 it returned to the emperor with the rest of the kingdom. The dictionary enters Pilsen because the Hussite wars are usually told as a nation against Rome, and Pilsen is the standing exception: a Czech-speaking royal town that judged the Four Articles and refused them, and whose refusal was a conviction and not a foreign garrison.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a siege as the setting of an army about a fortified place to take it; a press as a machine for printing; a league as an alliance or confederacy; and a garrison as a body of troops stationed in a fort.
webster_full: SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed; a machine for printing; the art or business of printing.
LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town to defend it.
RULE, v. To govern; to control the will and actions of others; to have authority over.
scriptures: Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Isa 2:18
And the idols he shall utterly abolish.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
In your patience possess ye your souls.
corruption_summary: Second city of Bohemia, Catholic capital through the Hussite wars, thrice besieged and never taken, and the site of the first printing press in the kingdom.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the partisan history that turns a reformation into a nation and then cannot explain the towns that said no. Pilsen was not a Habsburg outpost and not German-held; it was a Czech royal town that heard the Four Articles and judged them wrong, and it paid three sieges for the judgement. The dictionary holds that the Articles were substantially right and Pilsen substantially wrong, and records at the same time that the town's resistance was its own, because a history which cannot admit a sincere opponent cannot be trusted about a sincere friend either.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that both sides in a Christian quarrel are judged by the same rule, and the rule is not which side won the town. Prokop's army wore itself out before Pilsen and was broken at Lipany the next year, and “In your patience possess ye your souls” (Luk 21:19) was the counsel the Taborites most needed and least took. The magistrate on both sides “beareth not the sword in vain” (Rom 13:4), and the sword is given him for the punishing of evildoers and not for the settling of what the cup means.

pos: n. (the Moravian mining town, German Iglau, where the Compacts of Basel were solemnly proclaimed to the kingdom of Bohemia in 1436)
etymology: Czech Jihlava, from the river of that name, perhaps from jehla, a needle, for its sharp stones; German Iglau.
biblical_def: Jihlava is the town where the one formal agreement between Rome and a reforming body before Trent was read out and sworn. A German-speaking silver-mining town on the Bohemian-Moravian border, it was chosen as neutral ground, and on 5 July 1436 the Compacts negotiated at the Council of Basel were proclaimed there to the estates of Bohemia and Moravia: the laity of the kingdom might receive the cup, and the kingdom was received back into communion with the church. Sigismund was acknowledged king in the same place. The Compacts were the Hussites' victory and their defeat at once. They granted the cup and conceded nothing on the free preaching of the word, the holding of civil property by clergy, or the punishing of public sin, which were the other three of the Four Articles; and Rome never ratified what its legates at Basel had signed, Pius II declaring them void in 1462. Jihlava itself turned Lutheran in the sixteenth century and was recatholicised after 1620. The dictionary enters Jihlava because the Compacts are the first worked example of a reform settling for the concession it could get, and of what such a settlement is worth when the other party does not regard itself as bound.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a compact as an agreement between parties; to ratify as to confirm or establish; a concession as the act of yielding or granting; and union as the act of joining two or more things into one.
webster_full: COMPACT, n. An agreement; a contract between parties; a covenant or mutual engagement.
RATIFY, v. To confirm; to establish; to settle; to approve and sanction what has been done by an agent.
CONCESSION, n. The act of granting or yielding; usually implying a demand, claim or request from the party to whom it is made.
UNION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a compound body or a mixture.
AGREE, v. To be of one mind; to harmonize in opinion; to live in concord.
scriptures: Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise.
corruption_summary: Moravian mining town where the Compacts of Basel were proclaimed in 1436, granting the cup to the Bohemian laity and conceding nothing else.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the agreement that buys peace by leaving the doctrine unsettled. The Compacts gave the Bohemians the cup and left the mass, the priesthood, purgatory and the invocation of saints exactly as they were, and both parties signed knowing that the question of authority underneath had not been touched. “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) is the question the Compacts did not ask, and Pius II answered it in 1462 by declaring them void, which is what an unsettled agreement is always worth to the stronger party.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that unity is a unity in the truth confessed, not a formula that lets two doctrines stand. “that ye all speak the same thing” (1Co 1:10) is the standard, and it is met by agreement on what is believed and not by a licence to differ. Jihlava also teaches patience in the right place: the Brethren, who refused the Compacts as insufficient and had no settlement at all, were still a church in 1620 when the Utraquist establishment built on the Compacts had almost nothing left to lose, and of them it may be said that they had “need of patience” (Heb 10:36) and kept it.

pos: n. (the cluster of duchies north-east of Bohemia, Lutheran from the 1520s, and the land of the churches of peace and of grace)
etymology: Latin Silesia, German Schlesien, Polish Śląsk, from the river Slza or the Silingi who are said to have dwelt about Mount Zobten.
biblical_def: Silesia was a patchwork of duchies under the Bohemian crown, mostly German-speaking, and it took the Reformation faster and held it longer than any other Habsburg land. Breslau heard Lutheran preaching in 1518, and Frederick II of Legnica carried his duchy over in 1522 and founded a short-lived evangelical university at Liegnitz in 1526. Most of the duchies followed, and by 1600 Silesia was overwhelmingly Lutheran with Reformed and Schwenckfeldian minorities, Caspar Schwenckfeld himself being a Silesian nobleman whose spiritualising of the sacraments the Lutherans rejected. The Habsburg recovery after 1620 closed hundreds of churches, but Silesia was never fully recatholicised: the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 allowed three churches of peace, to be built outside the town walls of Glogau, Jauer and Schweidnitz of wood, clay and straw with no tower and no bell, and the Convention of Altranstadt in 1707, forced on the emperor by Charles XII of Sweden, allowed six more churches of grace. The dictionary enters Silesia because those timber churches, built to humiliating specifications and filled for generations, are the most exact picture in European history of a church permitted to exist on condition that it look like nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a duchy as the territory of a duke; a convention as an assembly or an agreement; grace as the free unmerited favour of God; and a tower as a lofty building of several stories.
webster_full: DUCHY, n. The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.
CONVENTION, n. The act of coming together; an assembly; also, an agreement or contract between parties.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God; the divine influence which renews the heart.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation and consisting of several stories.
TIMBER, n. That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, furniture and the like.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Zep 3:12
I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Duchies under the Bohemian crown, Lutheran from 1522, never fully recatholicised, and granted the timber churches of peace in 1648 and of grace in 1707.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the toleration that is really a humiliation, and Silesia is where it can be seen in its measurements. The churches of peace might be built of wood, clay and straw only, outside the walls, within a year, at the congregation's own cost, with no tower, no bell and no stone; the terms were written to make the Lutheran church of a Lutheran country look like a barn on sufferance. The congregations built them anyway, at Schweidnitz to hold seven thousand, and filled them for two centuries, which is the right answer to a humiliating permission.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church's dignity is not in its fabric and its security is not in its charter. “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10) was spoken to a congregation with no building at all. Silesia also shows the mercy that keeps a remnant where a settlement fails: “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9) is the Silesian case, for the three churches were a very small remnant of some fifteen hundred that had been taken away, and they were enough.

“a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9) — three churches permitted where fifteen hundred had been closed.
“an afflicted and poor people” (Zep 3:12) — timber, clay and straw, no tower and no bell.

pos: n. (the Wendish march between Saxony and Silesia, Lutheran from the Reformation, where Herrnhut was founded in 1722)
etymology: Latin Lusatia, German Lausitz, from the Sorbian łużica, a marshy place; divided into Upper and Lower Lusatia.
biblical_def: Lusatia is the march in which the Slavic Sorbs, called Wends by their German neighbours, kept a language of their own and received the Reformation in it. The Six Towns of Upper Lusatia and the estates of Lower Lusatia went Lutheran in the 1520s and 1530s, and because Lusatia was held of the Bohemian crown and then pledged to Lutheran Saxony in 1623, the Habsburg recatholicising which swallowed Bohemia stopped at its border. That border is why Lusatia matters. Sorbian preaching required Sorbian books, and the Reformation produced them: a Lower Sorbian New Testament by Mikawał Jakubica in 1548, Upper Sorbian catechisms and hymnals, and at length a complete Sorbian Bible, so that a people of perhaps two hundred thousand had Scripture in a tongue no empire valued. And on 17 June 1722 Christian David felled the first tree at Herrnhut on Count Zinzendorf's estate in Upper Lusatia, for the Moravian families who had crossed the mountains out of the hidden century; from that settlement went the Moravian missions to St Thomas in 1732, Greenland in 1733 and the Cape in 1737. The dictionary enters Lusatia because a small and despised language and a small and exiled congregation together produced more missionary labour than most kingdoms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tongue as the language spoken by a particular nation; a march as a border territory; a settlement as a place newly settled; and a mission as a sending with commission to preach.
webster_full: TONGUE, n. The language spoken by a particular nation; speech; the faculty or power of speaking.
MARCH, n. A border; a frontier; the confine or limit of a territory.
SETTLEMENT, n. The act of settling; a place newly settled; a colony or plantation.
MISSION, n. A sending; persons sent with commission, as to preach the gospel in heathen lands.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; the most retired part of the temple; a place of protection.

Therefore say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Although I have cast them far off among the heathen, and although I have scattered them among the countries, yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.

corruption_summary: The Wendish march between Saxony and Silesia, Lutheran from the 1520s, where Sorbian Scripture was printed and Herrnhut was founded in 1722.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the judgement that a small language is not worth a Bible. The Sorbs were a peasant people with no state, no court and no commercial use for their speech, and every argument of convenience said to preach to them in German. The Reformation's principle said otherwise, and the Lusatian ministers translated. “how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8) is the Pentecostal answer to the argument of convenience, and it is an answer that costs a translator a lifetime.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps a sanctuary for his people in the lands they are driven to, and sometimes makes it the base of a greater work than they lost. “yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come” (Eze 11:16) is what Herrnhut was for the Moravian refugees: a village of exiles which within fifteen years had men in the West Indies, Greenland and South Africa. The ones who came weeping with their seed did “come again with rejoicing” (Psa 126:6), though not to Moravia.

pos: n. (the Habsburg hereditary lands on the Danube, largely Lutheran by 1570 and wholly recatholicised by 1700)
etymology: Latin Austria, from Old High German Ostarrîchi, the eastern realm; German Österreich.
biblical_def: Austria is the land where the Reformation won the people and lost the prince, and where losing the prince proved to be decisive. By the 1570s the great majority of the Austrian nobility and of the burghers of Vienna, Linz and the Danube towns were Lutheran; the estates obtained the Religious Concession of 1568 and the Pacification of 1571, which allowed evangelical worship on noble estates, and Lutheran preaching was heard in Vienna within sight of the emperor's palace. There was no Austrian reformed church order, no Austrian confession and no Austrian synod; the evangelical cause rested on the estates' bargaining power and on preachers whom individual lords employed. When Ferdinand II came to the hereditary lands he dissolved it piece by piece: preachers expelled from 1598, reformation commissions with troops behind them, the nobility required after 1627 to conform or sell and emigrate, and the peasants left to be catechised by Jesuits. Tens of thousands left. Those who stayed became the crypto-Protestants of the Alpine valleys, keeping forbidden books for five generations until the Patent of Toleration of 1781 let them register. The dictionary enters Austria because it is the clearest case of a reformation that depended on patronage and was dismantled when the patrons were bought out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a patent as a writing granting a privilege; to conform as to comply with or yield obedience; emigration as removal from one country to another; and toleration as the allowance by law of religious opinions.
webster_full: PATENT, n. A writ or writing granting a privilege, or authenticating a right or title; letters patent.
CONFORM, v. To comply with or yield obedience to; to be obedient or submissive; to make like in manners or opinions.
EMIGRATION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.
TOLERATION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to those of the established church.
PATRON, n. A protector; a supporter; one who countenances or supports another.

And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Dan 2:21
And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:
corruption_summary: The Habsburg hereditary lands, largely Lutheran by 1570 under noble patronage, recatholicised by commission and emigration patent after 1598.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the church held by patronage, which is a landlord's church and falls with the landlord. Austria had evangelical preaching for two generations without ever building what Saxony and Scotland built: a confession the common people had learned, a catechising ministry in every parish, a synod able to meet and act. When Ferdinand required the nobility to conform or to emigrate, and most emigrated, the structure went with them, because the structure was their household chaplaincies. “the LORD shall scatter thee among all people” (Deu 28:64) came true in a land that had thought itself safe by treaty.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the crown is not the church's foundation, and that he who gives the crown takes it away. “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21) is the comfort of a people whose emperor has turned against them, and the Austrian crypto-Protestants lived on it for five generations with their books hidden in barns. Of them, as of the exiles who went down the Danube with what they could carry, it is written that “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11).

“he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21) — a reformation that rested on the prince and fell with him.

pos: n. (the Austrian duchy about Graz, Lutheran under its estates, where Ferdinand II served his apprenticeship in counter-reformation)
etymology: Latin Styria, German Steiermark, the march of Steyr, from the castle and town of that name on the Steyr river.
biblical_def: Styria is where the Habsburg counter-reformation was first worked out as a method, and where it was proved to work. The duchy was overwhelmingly Lutheran by 1570: the estates had their own church ordinance, a school and a ministry at Graz, and the Pacification of Bruck in 1578 confirmed evangelical worship for the nobility and the four chief towns. Archduke Charles conceded it and spent twenty years narrowing it. His son Ferdinand, educated by Jesuits at Ingolstadt, took the government in 1595, and from 1598 proceeded by a settled plan: close the Graz church and school, expel every evangelical preacher and schoolmaster on pain of death within fourteen days, send out reformation commissions with soldiers and a burning of books, require every burgher to conform or sell up, and leave the nobility for last. Among those expelled from the Graz school in 1600 was its mathematics master Johannes Kepler. By 1605 public Lutheranism in Styria was finished, and Ferdinand, who became emperor in 1619, applied in Bohemia and Austria what Styria had taught him. The dictionary enters Styria because the method, not the theology, is what destroyed the Austrian Reformation, and the method began here.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a commission as a warrant conferring authority; to expel as to drive out by force; an ordinance as a rule established by authority; and a schoolmaster as one who presides over a school.
webster_full: COMMISSION, n. A warrant or written authority, empowering a person to perform any act or exercise any jurisdiction.
EXPEL, v. To drive out; to force away; to eject; to banish.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; an established rite or ceremony.
SCHOOLMASTER, n. The man who presides over and teaches a school; a teacher or instructor.
PACIFICATION, n. The act of making peace between parties at variance; the act of appeasing.

They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
Psa 2:10

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
corruption_summary: Austrian duchy about Graz, Lutheran under the Pacification of 1578, cleared of evangelical ministry by Ferdinand's commissions after 1598.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is persecution carried out as administration, which is the form it usually takes and the form hardest to recognise. Nobody in Styria was burned for the gospel. Preachers were given fourteen days to leave, schoolmasters were dismissed, books were collected and burned, burghers were offered the choice of conformity or the sale of their property, and the whole was done by commission, under warrant, with the forms observed. “whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2) names the conscience behind it; the clerks who wrote the orders thought they were saving souls.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the promise of suffering is given to the godly as such and not only to the martyrs of the fire. “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12) covers the schoolmaster turned out of Graz with his family in winter as truly as it covers the stake. The warning belongs to the other party: “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10) was addressed to princes who thought a commission could settle what a man believes.

pos: n. (the southern Austrian duchy about Klagenfurt, Lutheran under its estates, and the home of the crypto-Protestants transmigrated to Transylvania)
etymology: Latin Carinthia, German Kärnten, Slovene Koroška, from the Celtic or Slavic name of the Carantani who dwelt there.
biblical_def: Carinthia is the Austrian duchy in which the forbidden church lasted longest, because its mountains were too many to police. Its estates were Lutheran from the 1540s and obtained with Styria and Carniola the Pacification of Bruck in 1578, and Klagenfurt had an evangelical church and school. Ferdinand's commissions closed them after 1600 by the Styrian method, and the nobility conformed or emigrated. What they could not do was empty the valleys. For a hundred and fifty years Carinthian peasants kept Lutheran postils, hymnbooks and Bibles hidden, met in houses and summer huts, taught their children to read on the forbidden books, and sent to Nuremberg and Regensburg for more; the authorities called them the house-readers, and the Jesuit missions sent among them reported whole parishes conforming outwardly and believing otherwise. In the 1730s and again under Maria Theresa the state answered with transmigration: some three thousand Carinthian and Upper Austrian Protestants were deported to Transylvania, where their descendants, the Landler, kept their speech and their confession into the twentieth century. The Patent of Toleration of 1781 found Lutheran congregations in Carinthia still able to constitute themselves at once. The dictionary enters Carinthia because it measures what a Bible in a farmhouse can hold for five generations with no minister at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a postil as a marginal note or a homily on the gospel; transmigration as a passing from one place or state into another; to deport as to transport or carry away; and a hut as a small cottage or mean lodge.
webster_full: POSTIL, n. A marginal note; a short exposition or homily upon the gospel or epistle of the day.
TRANSMIGRATION, n. The passing of a people from one country into another for the purpose of residence.
DEPORT, v. To transport; to carry away; to remove from one country to another by authority.
HUT, n. A small house, hovel or cabin; a mean lodge or cottage; a lodge for soldiers or herdsmen.
READER, n. One who reads; one whose office is to read prayers or the Scriptures in a congregation.

corruption_summary: Southern Austrian duchy about Klagenfurt, Lutheran from the 1540s, suppressed after 1600, kept by house-readers for five generations, and transmigrated to Transylvania.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the belief that a church cannot exist without its ministry, which the Carinthian valleys refute without denying the ministry's necessity. For a hundred and fifty years these people had no pastor, no sacrament rightly administered and no public assembly; they had a Bible, a hymnbook, a postil read aloud by a farmer, and the fifth commandment's duty of a father to teach his household. That is not a church order and the dictionary does not commend it as one. It is what is left when the church order is taken away by force, and it held.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the promise of a sanctuary in the place of exile and under the hand of the oppressor. “yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come” (Eze 11:16) was fulfilled twice over for the Carinthians, in the summer huts above their own villages and then in the Transylvanian villages they were deported to. Their patience was the thing commanded: “For ye have need of patience” (Heb 10:36), and in 1781 the congregations that constituted themselves within weeks showed what the patience had been keeping.
